response.title: How do I safely connect my electric car's power outlet to the house so I don't need extension cords everywhere during an outage?
response.answer:
The safest way is to install a dedicated generator inlet and a transfer switch (or approved interlock) so your electric car can power selected circuits through your home's existing wiring during an outage.

This lets you use your normal wall outlets and lights without running extension cords throughout the house.

However, there's an important distinction: an EV's 120V power outlet is not necessarily compatible with every generator transfer setup. You need to account for the car's power limit, grounding arrangement, and the electrical panel configuration.

1. How the setup works
Conceptual setup. The transfer equipment prevents the EV from energizing utility lines. Actual wiring and compatibility must be determined by an electrician.

An electrician can install an outdoor inlet connected to a transfer switch that supplies a small group of essential household circuits.

During an outage, you would connect the EV using the manufacturer-approved power output equipment and a properly rated cable, then activate the transfer equipment according to its instructions.

2. Choose the right equipment

Option

	

Best for

	

Important limitation




Manual transfer switch

	

A few essential circuits

	

Must be compatible with the EV's output




Panel interlock + inlet

	

More flexible circuit selection

	

Many conventional setups require 120/240V split-phase power




EV-specific home backup system

	

Higher-power or automatic backup

	

Requires vehicle-specific hardware and installation

For a car with only a standard 120V outlet, I would generally investigate a small, 120V-compatible manual transfer system first.

A typical 120V, 15A outlet provides a theoretical maximum of 1,800 watts, but the car may impose a lower continuous or total output limit.

3. What could you power?

Illustrative running loads — actual appliances vary

Refrigerator

150 W

LED lighting

80 W

Internet router

20 W

Laptop

65 W

TV

100 W

Example running total
415 W

Startup surges, especially from refrigerators, can be several times higher. This example does not establish that your car can safely supply these loads.
4. Critical safety precautions

Never backfeed a wall outlet. Do not use a male-to-male cable or connect the vehicle to a dryer outlet.

Never connect the EV directly to your panel without listed transfer equipment that isolates the utility supply.

Verify neutral and ground compatibility. Some EV inverter outlets have ground-fault protection or unusual neutral configurations that can trip or be unsafe with conventional transfer equipment.

Check 120V versus 240V compatibility. A 120V-only EV outlet cannot simply power both legs of a typical US split-phase panel.

Use a licensed electrician and obtain required permits. The equipment must be approved for the actual power source, not just for a conventional generator.

5. What I need to recommend the right setup
What electric car do you have? (make, model, year)
What power output does it have?
Standard 120V outlet
240V power output
Vehicle-to-Load (V2L) adapter
Not sure
What do you want to power?
Essential circuits (fridge, lights, Wi-Fi)
Most of the house
Find the right setup

The car model is especially important. Some EVs support a straightforward home-backup solution, while others have outlet and grounding restrictions that make a standard generator inlet unsuitable.
